difficulty_rationale: The presentation of irregular menses, hirsutism, acne, obesity, and impaired glucose tolerance strongly indicates PCOS, a common diagnosis familiar to general dermatologists.
Associating nail pitting with psoriasis and extensor silvery plaques is core dermatology knowledge commonly recalled by general dermatologists.
Classic presentation of tinea cruris in an athlete confirmed by KOH prep is core dermatology knowledge.
Identifying tinea versicolor by hypopigmented patches after sun exposure and confirming with KOH prep is core dermatology knowledge.
Identifying acral lentiginous melanoma as the most common melanoma subtype in individuals with darker skin is core dermatology knowledge.

Recognizing generalized erythroderma with patches/plaques and a >1 cm tumor (tumor stage) as cutaneous T-cell lymphoma/mycosis fungoides requires solid dermatology training and familiarity with lymphoma staging rather than basic derm knowledge.

Identifying IgM as the primary early humoral defense against an acute Staphylococcus aureus toxin-mediated infection requires immunology recall beyond routine dermatology knowledge, though the clinical diagnosis is straightforward.

Classic pediatric varicella presentation with pruritic lesions in multiple stages (macules, papules, vesicles, crusts) and mild prodrome, distinguishing it readily from measles, rubella, and contact dermatitis.

Classic herpes zoster presentation with a unilateral dermatomal vesicular rash and burning pain, attributed to varicella-zoster virus reactivation in dorsal root ganglia, is core knowledge for general dermatology.
Knowing that combined oral contraceptives reduce ovarian (and endometrial) cancer risk is core general medical knowledge relevant to dermatology when prescribing for acne.
Classic presentation of lower lip painless nonhealing ulcer in an older smoker with chronic sun exposure strongly indicates squamous cell carcinoma, a core dermatologic diagnosis.
Recognizing that urticarial wheals from IgE-mediated histamine release involve dermal edema rather than epidermal layers is core dermatology knowledge.
Identifying vitiligo by the hallmark histology of absent epidermal melanocytes is core dermatology knowledge and distinguishes it clearly from tinea versicolor and albinism.
Recognizing leprosy (Mycobacterium leprae) from thickened facial skin and peripheral neuropathy and knowing mycobacteria are acid-fast is core dermatology knowledge.
Classic presentation of xeroderma pigmentosum with severe photosensitivity and ocular involvement, directly linked to defective nucleotide excision repair.

Recognizing FOXP3 mutation with Treg defect as IPEX syndrome and linking it to autoimmune endocrinopathy requires solid training beyond basic dermatology despite classic associations with eczema and chronic diarrhea.
Recognizing actinic keratosis on a sun-exposed scalp of an older man with significant cumulative UV exposure is a classic, high-frequency presentation familiar to any general dermatologist.
Classic presentation and histology of a rapidly growing dome-shaped lesion with central keratin plug in a sun-exposed elderly patient points clearly to keratoacanthoma, a core dermatology diagnosis.
Classic bullous pemphigoid presentation with linear IgG at the basement membrane pointing to hemidesmosomes is core dermatology knowledge.

Classic features of antiphospholipid syndrome—recurrent early miscarriages, livedo reticularis, and superficial thrombophlebitis—point to anticardiolipin antibodies, a core association most dermatologists readily recall.
Identifying color variegation as a classic ABCDE feature of melanoma is core dermatology knowledge that most general dermatologists recall readily.

Recognizing mixed connective tissue disease requires integrating Raynaud’s phenomenon with myositis signs and the specific serology of anti-U1 RNP, a step beyond basic core knowledge but familiar to well-trained dermatologists.

Identifying lamotrigine as the cause requires recalling its association with erythema multiforme/Stevens-Johnson–like targetoid eruptions after initiation, distinguishing it from other bipolar treatments less commonly linked to acute target lesions.
Classic warfarin-induced skin necrosis shortly after initiation in a patient with risk factors, treated with protein C replacement is core knowledge for general dermatologists.

Classic presentation of herpetic whitlow in a healthcare worker with grouped tender vesicles on a finger, for which oral acyclovir is standard management that general dermatologists readily recognize.
Classic tinea corporis confirmed by KOH hyphae should be treated with an antifungal; recognizing itraconazole (a systemic antifungal) over antibiotics is straightforward core knowledge.

Recognizing cat scratch disease from linear inoculation lesions, regional lymphadenopathy, and necrotizing granulomas and linking Bartonella henselae to bacillary angiomatosis requires solid training beyond basic dermatology knowledge.
Central umbilicated, dome-shaped papules are classic for molluscum contagiosum and should be readily recognized by any general dermatologist.
Recognition of a firm hyperpigmented papule with dimpling on lateral compression (dimple sign) is a classic, high-yield feature of dermatofibroma that general dermatologists readily recall.
Classic presentation of rosacea triggered by sun/heat with central facial erythema is commonly managed first-line with topical metronidazole, a core treatment most dermatologists recall readily.

Recognizing acrodermatitis enteropathica–like findings (periorificial bullous plaques, alopecia) plus dysgeusia and malabsorption after small bowel resection as zinc deficiency requires integrating multiple clinical clues beyond basic dermatology knowledge.

Recognizing that chronic systemic corticosteroid use increases risk of osteoporosis and fragility fractures—classically hip (femoral neck) and vertebral—is core knowledge for general dermatologists who commonly prescribe steroids.
Classic presentation of tinea cruris with pruritic, well-demarcated inguinal rash sparing the scrotum in a wrestler, a core diagnosis for general dermatologists.
Identifying varicella in an unvaccinated toddler with pruritic rash starting on the trunk and spreading, typically with lesions in different stages, is core pediatric dermatology knowledge.

Classic presentation of ichthyosis vulgaris with childhood onset, winter worsening, sparing of flexures, follicular hyperkeratosis, and palmar hyperlinearity—core knowledge for general dermatologists.

Identifying an acute urticarial drug reaction from pruritic wheals after starting an antibiotic and linking it to superficial dermal edema due to increased vascular permeability is core dermatology knowledge.
Recognizing perianal pruritus with positive scotch tape test as Enterobius vermicularis and knowing pyrantel pamoate as an alternative to albendazole is core, commonly tested knowledge.
Computing number needed to treat from trial cure rates (ARR = 190/250 − 165/250 = 25/250, NNT = 1/ARR = 250/25) is basic clinical epidemiology knowledge expected of general dermatologists.
Classic erythema nodosum presentation in a child following recent pharyngitis, with throat culture as the straightforward next step to evaluate streptococcal trigger.
A delayed 48-hour indurated skin reaction to Candida is a classic delayed-type (Type IV) hypersensitivity mediated by CD4+ T cells, a core immunology concept familiar to general dermatologists.

Identifying Pseudomonas aeruginosa from hot-tub folliculitis based on non-lactose fermenting, oxidase-positive gram-negative rods and associating it with blue-green pigment is core, classic dermatology/infectious disease knowledge.
The malar rash sparing nasolabial folds and oral ulcers strongly indicate systemic lupus erythematosus, for which lymphopenia is a classic and commonly recalled hematologic abnormality.
Recognizing aldesleukin (IL-2) as an immunotherapy for metastatic melanoma that activates NK cells and cytotoxic T cells is core pharmacology commonly known to general dermatologists.

Identifying drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis from NSAID use with eosinophilia and WBC casts and linking it to the classic triad including a diffuse maculopapular rash requires solid training and pattern recognition beyond basic dermatology.

Identifying chronic granulomatous disease based on recurrent skin abscesses with pus, lymphadenopathy, and recurrent infections requires immunology knowledge and distinguishing it from other pediatric immunodeficiencies and atopic dermatitis.

Classic presentation of lymphogranuloma venereum after a transient painless genital ulcer followed by painful unilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy, with diagnosis by Chlamydia trachomatis testing—a core STI-derm association familiar to general dermatologists.

Classic presentation of a painful, purulent genital ulcer with painful inguinal lymphadenopathy points to chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi), a core STD differentiation from HSV and syphilis that general dermatologists routinely know.
Classic photodistributed fragile blisters with hypertrichosis suggest porphyria cutanea tarda, confirmed by elevated urine porphyrins—core knowledge for general dermatologists.
Classic description of seborrheic keratoses as brown, greasy, “stuck-on” lesions in an elderly patient is core dermatology knowledge.
Identifying nickel-induced allergic contact dermatitis from earrings as a type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction is core dermatology knowledge.
Classic presentation of bullous pemphigoid in an elderly patient with tense, non-fragile bullae and linear IgG/C3 at the basement membrane—core knowledge for general dermatologists.
Classic hot-tub folliculitis from Pseudomonas after whirlpool exposure presents with pustular rash on trunk/thighs arising from hair follicles, a core dermatology concept.
Identifying genital warts from acetic acid whitening and exophytic papules and knowing HPV vaccination prevents them is standard core knowledge for general dermatologists.

Identifying a phototoxic drug reaction from tetracycline-class medication (demeclocycline) after brief sun exposure is core dermatology knowledge involving classic presentation and mechanism of direct cell injury by reactive drug metabolites.
Classic presentation of psoriatic arthritis with DIP involvement, nail pitting, psoriatic plaques on elbows, and family history—core knowledge for general dermatology.
Identifying elevated TSH as the most helpful diagnostic finding for primary hypothyroidism with classic symptoms is core endocrinology-dermatology knowledge any general dermatologist would recall.

Requires distinguishing PCOS from nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia using specific hormone patterns (elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone with mild hyperandrogenism), which goes beyond basic knowledge into nuanced endocrinologic reasoning.
Classic neonatal presentation with fever, diffuse erythema, flaccid bullae, positive Nikolsky sign, and mucosal sparing points straightforwardly to staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome.

Classic postmenopausal presentation of lichen sclerosus with pruritus, porcelain-white atrophic plaques, labia minora loss, clitoral phimosis, and perianal involvement is well-known to general dermatologists.

Classic SLE presentation with malar rash sparing nasolabial folds, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, and small-joint arthritis, pointing to lupus nephritis (proliferative GN) as the likely additional finding is core knowledge for general dermatologists.

Classic pilonidal abscess presentation with fever and tender, erythematous swelling over the natal cleft where first-line management is incision and drainage, a core management point for general dermatologists.

Identifying that the acne treatment requiring contraception is isotretinoin and recognizing its structural similarity to all-trans retinoic acid used for acute promyelocytic leukemia requires specific pharmacologic recall beyond basic dermatology knowledge.
Identifying topical benzoyl peroxide as first-line therapy for comedonal, mild acne is core dermatology knowledge.

Recognizing Gottron papules with proximal muscle weakness as dermatomyositis and recalling that anti–histidyl tRNA synthetase (anti–Jo-1) is a myositis-specific antibody requires solid training beyond basic dermatology, distinguishing it from other autoantibodies tied to drug-induced lupus, primary biliary cholangitis, or statin myopathy.
Classic presentation of bullous pemphigoid (tense bullae, negative Nikolsky sign, no mucosal involvement) with antibodies to hemidesmosomes is core dermatology knowledge.
This tests the classic association of warfarin-induced skin necrosis with protein C deficiency, a well-known core concept for general dermatologists.
Recognizing spider angiomas in chronic liver disease and attributing them to estrogen excess (hormonal imbalance) is core dermatology knowledge commonly recalled by general dermatologists.
Identifying allergic contact dermatitis from new gloves and selecting patch testing as the next step is core dermatology knowledge for evaluating hand dermatitis.

Identifying early localized Lyme disease with erythema migrans in a child and selecting age-appropriate first-line therapy (amoxicillin rather than doxycycline or macrolides/penicillins) requires solid training and regional epidemiology knowledge beyond basic dermatology.
Classic description of basal cell carcinoma with pearly papule, rolled borders, and telangiectasias on sun-exposed eyelid in a fair-skinned older man is core dermatology knowledge.
Recognizing dermatitis herpetiformis with GI symptoms suggestive of celiac disease and confirming with anti-tTG/gliadin antibodies is core dermatology knowledge.

Classic presentation of alopecia areata with smooth non-scarring patches and positive hair pull test, easily distinguished from syphilis, tinea capitis, and trichotillomania by a general dermatologist.

Identifying subungual melanoma versus more common mimickers like traumatic hemorrhage or onychomycosis requires nuanced recognition of nail apparatus melanoma features (eg, longitudinal melanonychia with periungual spread) beyond basic dermatology knowledge.
Classic allergic contact dermatitis from poison ivy with linear vesicles after hiking is routinely treated with high-potency topical corticosteroids like clobetasol for localized disease.

Recognizing uncomplicated first-degree/superficial sunburn after sun exposure and treating with supportive care (cooling, emollients like aloe, not antibiotics or aggressive fluids) is core dermatology knowledge.
Identifying impetigo in a healthy child and choosing topical mupirocin as first-line therapy is core pediatric dermatology knowledge for general dermatologists.

Classic presentation of chromoblastomycosis with cauliflower-like verrucous plaques in a barefoot tropical farmer and KOH showing sclerotic (Medlar) bodies, a hallmark most dermatologists readily recognize.
Classic painless penile chancre with bilateral nontender inguinal lymphadenopathy indicates primary syphilis due to Treponema pallidum, a core diagnosis for general dermatologists.

Classic presentation of lower-lip squamous cell carcinoma in an older male with sun and tobacco exposure and a nonhealing ulcer with everted, friable edges, which any general dermatologist should recognize.
Identifying Staphylococcus aureus in impetigo and recalling Protein A as the IgG Fc-binding antiphagocytic factor is core, well-known dermatology and microbiology knowledge.
Classic ecthyma gangrenosum in a febrile, neutropenic patient on chemotherapy with necrotic ulcers and violaceous margins strongly points to Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a well-known core association.
Recognizing sudden-onset acanthosis nigricans as a paraneoplastic sign of gastric adenocarcinoma is core dermatology knowledge, contrasted with the more common obesity/diabetes-associated form.
Classic presentation of tinea capitis in a child with patchy alopecia, black dots, posterior cervical/occipital lymphadenopathy, and scalp scaling—core knowledge for general dermatologists.
Recognizing contagious, umbilicated papules in young children as molluscum contagiosum due to poxvirus is core dermatology knowledge.
Classic presentation of recurrent, rough, scaly lesions on sun-exposed dorsal hands in an older outdoor worker strongly indicates actinic keratosis, a core diagnosis for general dermatologists.

Identifying a chronic, painless, ulcerated penile lesion in a high-risk patient as squamous cell carcinoma in situ/invasive SCC and recognizing atypical squamous cells with mitoses on biopsy reflects core dermatologic-oncologic knowledge with classic risk factors and presentation.
Recognizing isoniazid-induced drug reaction from slow acetylators (N-acetyltransferase deficiency) requires specific pharmacogenetic knowledge beyond basic dermatology.
Classic pediatric atopic dermatitis in flexural areas is strongly associated with atopy, including asthma characterized by a reversible decrease in FEV1/FVC.

Recognizing neurofibromatosis type 1 from café-au-lait macules, neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules and knowing to screen for optic pathway glioma with brain/orbit MRI requires solid training beyond basic dermatology, though still common enough for general dermatologists.

Clustered pruritic rash with nocturnal itch and multiple affected residents in a nursing home sparing groin suggests bed bug bites (Cimex lectularius), a classic presentation familiar to general dermatologists.

Classic presentation of Rocky Mountain spotted fever with fever followed by a rash starting on wrists/ankles and spreading to trunk including palms/soles, a hallmark pattern well-known to general dermatologists.
Recognizing a painless chancre with nontender lymphadenopathy as primary syphilis and confirming with dark-field microscopy is core, classic knowledge for general dermatology.
Classic roseola presentation with high fever in an infant followed by a maculopapular rash after defervescence is core pediatric dermatology knowledge.
Classic allergic contact dermatitis from poison ivy after outdoor exposure presents with pruritic papules/vesicles and is mediated by type IV hypersensitivity with T-cell–mediated cytotoxicity.
Recognizing acanthosis nigricans in an obese young woman and linking it to insulin resistance and PCOS is core dermatology knowledge.
Classic Kaposi sarcoma presentation in an HIV patient with spindle cells on biopsy pointing to HHV-8 is core dermatology knowledge.
Classic hand-foot-and-mouth disease presentation with oral vesicles and rash on hands/feet in a child points to Coxsackie A virus, a core pediatric dermatology diagnosis.

Identifying intertrigo due to Candida in obese skin folds with pruritic, erythematous, macerated rash is classic core knowledge and distinguishing it from Pseudomonas, Cryptococcus, or mycobacteria is straightforward for a general dermatologist.
Classic slapped-cheek and lacy reticular rash of erythema infectiosum is hallmark for Parvovirus B19, a core pediatric exanthem recognition for general dermatologists.
Classic tuberous sclerosis complex presentation (facial angiofibromas, hypomelanotic macules, enamel pits, seizures/developmental delay) directly points to TSC gene mutations.

Recognizing lichen sclerosus from clinical and histologic clues and linking it specifically to increased risk of differentiated vulvar SCC (rather than HPV-related HSIL/LSIL or BCC) requires solid dermatology training and nuanced knowledge of vulvar oncology associations.
Classic plaque psoriasis presentation with extensor involvement, dactylitis, and RF-negative arthritis makes ‘silver, scaly’ straightforward for any general dermatologist.

Recognizing Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome from the triad of eczema, recurrent infections, and thrombocytopenia with petechiae requires pediatric immunodeficiency knowledge beyond routine dermatology, though the eczematous and petechial clues are clinically familiar.

Recognizing vitiligo from depigmented macules with Wood’s lamp accentuation and association with autoimmune thyroid disease is core dermatology knowledge distinguishing it from hypopigmented/infectious mimickers.
Classic PKU vignette (intellectual disability, fair skin/blue eyes, eczema, myoclonic jerks) pointing to phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency is core dermatology-pediatrics knowledge.
Identifying trichotillomania in an adolescent with irregular broken hairs and stress/obsessive behaviors and knowing CBT is first-line is core knowledge for general dermatologists.

Classic slapped-cheek and lacy reticular body rash in a toddler after mild prodrome strongly indicates erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19), a hallmark pediatric exanthem well known to general dermatologists.
Classic presentation of perianal and vulvar pruritus in a young child suggests Enterobius vermicularis, for which the perianal cellophane-tape test is the standard diagnostic step.
Classic scabies presentation with nocturnal pruritus and interdigital burrows in a child; first-line treatment with topical permethrin is core dermatology knowledge.
Classic herpetic whitlow following genital HSV exposure; identifying HSV as an enveloped, double-stranded linear DNA virus is core dermatology knowledge.

Recognizing porphyria cutanea tarda and knowing phlebotomy is first-line (especially with normal ferritin nuance vs alternatives like low-dose hydroxychloroquine) requires solid dermatology training beyond basic knowledge.
Umbilicated, skin-colored papules in an HIV patient are classic for molluscum contagiosum caused by a poxvirus, a core dermatology diagnosis.
Classic presentation of pemphigus vulgaris with flaccid mucocutaneous blisters and positive Nikolsky sign, requiring recall that autoantibodies target desmoglein cadherins in desmosomes.
Recognizing drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis from a recent thiazide exposure with rash, hematuria, AKI, and classic urinary eosinophils is core clinical knowledge for general dermatologists.
Recognizing Kaposi sarcoma in an HIV patient from violaceous lesions and spindle cells on biopsy and knowing interferon-α is an appropriate therapy is core dermatology knowledge.
Classic presentation of tinea corporis in a wrestler; confirming with a bedside KOH preparation is core dermatology knowledge.
Linking café-au-lait macules and axillary freckling to NF1 and recognizing iris hamartomas (Lisch nodules) as the associated finding is core dermatology knowledge.

Classic sporotrichosis from rose-thorn injury with nodular lymphangitis and treatment with itraconazole (ergosterol synthesis inhibitor) and possible gynecomastia is well-known core dermatology knowledge.
Recognizing UVB-induced pyrimidine (thymidine) dimers as the classic DNA lesion leading to cutaneous SCC is core dermatology knowledge.
Classic presentation of sporotrichosis with nodular lesions ascending along lymphatics after gardening injury is well-known to general dermatologists.
Recognizing tinea versicolor from hypopigmented macules on the trunk that don’t tan and are caused by Malassezia is core dermatology knowledge.
Classic presentation of pemphigus vulgaris with flaccid bullae, positive Nikolsky sign, and mucosal involvement, caused by anti–desmoglein-3 antibodies—core dermatology knowledge.
Classic psoriasis presentation with Auspitz sign where diagnosis is clinical and no testing is required.
Classic measles presentation with Koplik spots and cephalocaudal spread; identifying measles as an enveloped, single-stranded RNA paramyxovirus is core knowledge for general dermatologists.

Identifying pyoderma gangrenosum requires recognizing its classic rapidly progressive, painful ulcer with undermined violaceous borders and association with IBD while excluding mimics like ecthyma gangrenosum or blastomycosis.

Identifying bullous photosensitivity after sun exposure as a heme synthesis disorder and recalling that uroporphyrinogen III accumulates in porphyria cutanea tarda requires specific biochemical-pathologic linkage beyond routine dermatology knowledge.

Identifying malignant melanoma from a changing, enlarging pigmented lesion with partial elevation and lack of dimpling is core dermatology knowledge and distinguishes it from common mimickers like keratoacanthoma, lentigo maligna, and basal cell carcinoma.

Identifying erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19) by its classic slapped-cheek rash followed by lacy reticular body rash and confirming with parvovirus IgM/IgG serology is core pediatric exanthem knowledge for general dermatologists.

The description of Wickham striae and pruritic rash points to lichen planus, for which interface dermatitis with band-like lymphocytes at the dermoepidermal junction is a classic, well-known finding to general dermatologists.

Classic triad of disseminated gonococcal infection—migratory polyarthralgia/tenosynovitis, pustular acral lesions, and minimal fever—makes this a straightforward recognition problem for a general dermatologist.

Recognizing NF1 from café-au-lait spots and Lisch nodules and then recalling its associated tumor risk (pheochromocytoma) requires solid dermatology training beyond basic knowledge, though it is a common board topic.
Associating maternal secondary syphilis (positive RPR, palmar rash, darkfield confirmation) with congenital syphilis stigmata like saddle nose is core, widely known prenatal dermatology knowledge.

Classic pediatric atopic dermatitis with periocular/perioral pruritic eczematous plaques and personal atopy (asthma), distinguishing it from impetigo, conjunctivitis, or SSSS is straightforward for a general dermatologist.
Recognizing isoniazid as the classic cause of drug-induced lupus with positive anti-histone antibodies in a TB regimen is core dermatology/pharmacology knowledge.

Classic slapped-cheek rash sparing perioral area followed by lacy reticular exanthem on trunk/extremities after mild viral prodrome is a hallmark presentation of erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19) familiar to general dermatologists.

Recognizing ACE inhibitor–induced angioedema (lip swelling) after starting antihypertensive therapy is classic core knowledge for general dermatologists, distinguishing it from edema with calcium channel blockers or diuretics.

Identifying the need for a pregnancy test before initiating systemic acne therapies (eg, doxycycline, isotretinoin, or hormonal agents) in a sexually active adolescent is standard, core dermatology practice.
Recognizing hyperlipidemia as the major side effect of systemic retinoids (isotretinoin) for acne is core dermatology knowledge.
Classic slapped-cheek/lacy rash of erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19) with circumoral pallor, whose hallmark is tropism for erythroid progenitor cells—core pediatric/dermatology knowledge.
Identifying Breslow depth (tumor thickness) as the single most important prognostic factor in melanoma is core dermatology knowledge.

Identifying mycosis fungoides/Sézary syndrome from pruritic scaly patches with epidermotropic cerebriform neoplastic cells and recognizing it as a cutaneous T-cell lymphoma is core dermatology knowledge.

Classic measles presentation with cough-coryza-conjunctivitis, high fever, cephalocaudal rash, and recent immigration with unknown vaccination; recognizing vitamin A supplementation as standard management is core pediatric/dermatology knowledge.

Recognizing cutaneous leishmaniasis with ulcerative plaque after Central American travel and lymphadenopathy requires knowledge of regional parasitology and distinguishing it from other tropical infections, beyond core everyday dermatology.
Classic presentation of roseola with high fever and febrile seizure followed by a blanching trunk-to-extremity rash in an infant, a core pediatric derm diagnosis.

Identifying uncomplicated primary varicella with pruritic vesicles in various stages and choosing supportive care (e.g., calamine lotion) is core pediatric dermatology knowledge for general dermatologists.
Recognizing spongiosis (intraepidermal edema with widened intercellular spaces) as the histologic hallmark of eczematous dermatitis is core dermatopathology knowledge for general dermatologists.
Classic presentation of tinea versicolor with hypopigmented macules and fine scale after sun exposure, caused by Malassezia overgrowth—core knowledge for general dermatologists.
Recognizing Stevens-Johnson syndrome from acute onset of targetoid macules progressing to bullae/epidermal detachment with mucosal involvement after new medications is core dermatology knowledge.
Classic presentation of psoriasis with nail pitting and symmetric inflammatory arthritis with negative RF/ANA strongly indicates psoriatic arthritis, a core diagnosis for general dermatologists.
Recognizing onychomycosis and knowing that oral terbinafine is first-line with risk of hepatotoxicity is core dermatology knowledge.

Classic presentation of a subungual glomus tumor—cold sensitivity, severe point tenderness, blue-red subungual papule—arising from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body is core dermatology knowledge.

Classic painless pruritic papule progressing to vesicle then ulcer with black eschar, significant edema, low-grade fever, and painless regional lymphadenopathy points to cutaneous anthrax, for which wool handling (exposure to animal hides) is a well-known, core risk factor.

Recognizing riboflavin deficiency from seborrheic dermatitis–like facial rash, angular cheilitis, glossitis, normocytic anemia, and elevated erythrocyte glutathione reductase requires solid training in nutritional dermatoses and vitamin biochemistry (linking to FAD), beyond routine dermatology basics.

Distinguishing Bowen's disease from erythroplasia of Queyrat and Bowenoid papulosis on the basis of location (keratinized shaft vs glans), morphology, and biopsy features requires nuanced clinical-pathologic correlation beyond basic knowledge.
Recognizing the iPLEDGE requirement for two negative pregnancy tests before initiating isotretinoin is fundamental, widely emphasized core knowledge for any practicing dermatologist.

Identifying tabes dorsalis (neurosyphilis) presenting with positive Romberg's sign from a history of untreated syphilis requires recalling specific neurologic sequelae and distinguishing among plausible neurologic findings.

Recognizing bacillary angiomatosis in an untreated HIV patient from clinical and histologic clues and knowing macrolides like erythromycin are first-line requires solid dermatology training beyond basic knowledge.
Selecting local anesthesia for an outpatient excision of a moderately sized basal cell carcinoma on the back is standard core practice for general dermatologists.
Recognizing UV-B as the primary cause of sunburn on sun-exposed areas is core dermatology knowledge.

Recognizing pellagra from photosensitivity dermatitis plus neurologic signs and linking it to defective tryptophan absorption (e.g., Hartnup disease) and low niacin requires integrated, less-common vitamin deficiency knowledge beyond everyday dermatology.
Classic tinea corporis in a teen with gardening exposure and annular pruritic rash is straightforward, with topical antifungal (clotrimazole) as first-line therapy.
Classic description of molluscum contagiosum with pearly, umbilicated papules in a young child and daycare exposure is core knowledge for general dermatologists.
Classic early Lyme disease after tick exposure with erythema migrans and systemic symptoms, for which doxycycline is the well-known first-line treatment.
Recognizing acute photosensitivity from a tetracycline (demeclocycline) after brief sun exposure is core dermatology knowledge with a classic presentation and common medication culprit.

Recognizing and managing serum sickness–like reaction to heterologous antivenom with systemic corticosteroids plus antihistamines requires specific, less-common knowledge beyond routine dermatology practice.
Classic linear/clustered pruritic papules in rows (“breakfast, lunch, and dinner”) after travel strongly indicate bed bug bites, a common presentation familiar to general dermatologists.
Classic painless, indurated genital ulcer suggests primary syphilis caused by motile, helical Treponema pallidum, a core STI presentation familiar to general dermatologists.

Identifying an acute, itchy, blanchable urticarial eruption due to mast cell degranulation (histamine-mediated) is core dermatology knowledge and distinguishes readily from psoriasis, tinea, or ACE-inhibitor–related bradykinin angioedema.

Recognizing tendon xanthomas and linking them to lipoprotein extravasation in familial hypercholesterolemia is a step beyond basic knowledge and requires distinguishing from gouty tophi or rheumatoid nodules.

Selecting 1–2 cm margins and adding sentinel lymph node biopsy for a 1.1 mm melanoma requires recall of staging-based margin guidelines and SLNB indications, which go beyond basic knowledge but are standard for trained dermatologists.
Classic infantile seborrheic dermatitis presentation with greasy yellow scales on scalp/hairline in a comfortable infant is straightforward for any general dermatologist.

Identifying vitiligo by depigmented, asymptomatic patches and recognizing its autoimmune melanocyte destruction is core dermatology knowledge, distinguishing it from albinism, tinea versicolor, and leprosy.

Classic histopathology of psoriasis (thinned/absent granular layer with parakeratosis and neutrophils in the stratum corneum) linked to its well-known association with seronegative spondyloarthropathy.
Recognizing histamine as the mediator of immediate wheal-and-flare reactions after an insect bite is fundamental dermatologic knowledge.

Classic presentation of tinea versicolor with hypopigmented, finely scaly macules and positive scraping after tropical travel points to Malassezia overgrowth, a core diagnosis for general dermatologists.
Classic presentation of staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome in an infant with positive Nikolsky sign and perioral onset, requiring recall that exfoliative toxins cleave desmoglein-1.

Recognizing SLE with possible lupus nephritis despite bland urine sediment and indicating renal biopsy based on significant proteinuria and cytopenias requires nuanced knowledge of nephritis evaluation and biopsy indications beyond basic lupus recognition.
Recognizing tetracyclines like minocycline are contraindicated in pregnancy due to fetal tooth discoloration and inhibition of bone growth is core dermatologic/pharmacologic knowledge.
Classic presentation of leprosy with anesthetic hypopigmented patches, eyebrow/eyelash loss, peripheral neuropathy, and endemic setting—core knowledge for general dermatology.
Classic pediatric varicella presentation with pruritic vesicles in multiple stages and school outbreak; knowing bacterial superinfection is the most common complication is core dermatology knowledge.
Classic description of a rough, sandpaper-like scaly plaque on sun-exposed skin in an older sunbather strongly indicates actinic keratosis, a core diagnosis for general dermatologists.
Identifying variegated color as a malignant sign relies on the basic ABCDE criteria for melanoma, which is core knowledge for any general dermatologist.
The triad of eczema, recurrent infections, and thrombocytopenia is a classic board-level association for Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome that general dermatologists are expected to recall readily.
Recognizing serpiginous, intensely pruritic rash after travel to tropical regions as cutaneous larva migrans is a classic, high-yield presentation familiar to general dermatologists.

Recognizing trichotillomania (hair pulling with short broken hairs and nail changes in an anxious adolescent) and knowing behavioral therapy is first-line is standard core knowledge for general dermatologists.
Classic presentation of pemphigus vulgaris with flaccid blisters, mucosal involvement, positive Nikolsky sign, and appropriate differentials that a general dermatologist would readily distinguish.

Identifying immersion scald burn patterns suggestive of nonaccidental trauma and linking them to likely additional findings (multiple injuries in different healing stages) requires nuanced clinical reasoning beyond basic dermatology knowledge.
Recognizing malar rash, photosensitivity, and arthritis as SLE and associating chest pain relief by sitting forward with pericarditis is core, widely known knowledge for general dermatologists.

Recognizing classic psoriasis with associated arthropathy and conjunctival involvement and recalling its hallmark histology (acanthosis with elongated rete ridges, increased dermal capillaries, and hyperkeratosis/parakeratosis) is core dermatology knowledge.
Classic early disseminated Lyme disease with erythema migrans and migratory arthralgias; recognizing cranial nerve palsy (e.g., facial nerve) as a common complication is core dermatology knowledge.

Classic allergic contact dermatitis from poison ivy/oak after woodland exposure with vesicles and pruritus is a prototypical Type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction that general dermatologists recognize readily.

Requires recognizing serum sickness–like reaction in a child after amoxicillin with fever, arthralgias, pruritic annular/urticarial plaques lasting >24 hours and periorbital edema while distinguishing from SJS and DRESS, which is a nuanced clinical differentiation beyond core basics.

Classic presentation of leprosy with acid-fast bacilli and nerve involvement, for which dapsone is a well-known first-line treatment in standard multidrug therapy.

Identifying erythema toxicum neonatorum from a classic presentation (day 2–5 onset, erythematous macules/papules with pustules sparing palms/soles in a well newborn) is core pediatric dermatology knowledge for general dermatologists.

Recognizing onchocerciasis requires linking pruritic papular dermatitis, visual decline, subcutaneous nodules, endemic exposure, and skin snip microfilariae—knowledge beyond basic derm, but standard for a well-trained dermatologist.

Recognizing Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis spectrum from the clinical scenario and medication trigger is core, but knowing that confirmation is by routine histopathology (showing full-thickness epidermal necrosis with minimal inflammation) rather than direct immunofluorescence or culture requires more nuanced diagnostic knowledge.
Classic rosacea presentation with facial erythema, telangiectasias, and papules without comedones; first-line therapy is topical metronidazole, which most general dermatologists know readily.

Recognizing erythema nodosum and knowing to evaluate for underlying causes—particularly sarcoidosis with a screening chest x-ray despite normal ASO—requires solid training beyond basic first-line management.
Selecting oral isotretinoin for severe nodulocystic, scarring acne is a core, first-line decision every general dermatologist should know.
Classic presentation of staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome in a young child with positive Nikolsky sign and tender erythema points directly to Staphylococcus aureus, a core dermatology diagnosis.

Classic presentation of hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia with mucocutaneous telangiectasias and epistaxis, where AVMs can cause high-output cardiac failure is core knowledge for general dermatologists.

Identifying tinea pedis from moist boot use and disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol points to griseofulvin, whose mechanism is mitotic spindle inhibition causing cell arrest at metaphase—core dermatology pharmacology knowledge.

Identifying an Arthus reaction (immune complex deposition) presenting as a localized ulcer and induration after immunization requires recognizing a less-common vaccine reaction and distinguishing it from more familiar immediate hypersensitivity or infectious complications.

Classic, high-yield presentation of toxic epidermal necrolysis with medication trigger, >30% BSA involvement, mucosal involvement, and positive Nikolsky sign—core knowledge for general dermatologists.

Identifying lamotrigine as a classic trigger for Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis in a child with acute painful targetoid rash and mucosal involvement is core dermatology knowledge.
Classic erythema migrans with target-like expanding patch, low-grade fever, regional lymphadenopathy, and recent camping strongly points to Lyme disease—core knowledge for general dermatologists.

Identifying Felty syndrome requires recognizing the triad of long-standing rheumatoid arthritis, neutropenia, and splenomegaly with leg ulcers and excluding venous stasis, which is a nuanced clinical association beyond basic dermatology knowledge.
Recognizing that high-potency topical corticosteroids (which inhibit NF-κB and phospholipase A2) can cause dermal collagen loss/atrophy with long-term use is core dermatology knowledge.

Classic pediatric presentation of staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome with fever, flaccid easily ruptured blisters, positive Nikolsky sign, and no mucosal involvement—core knowledge for general dermatologists.

Classic drug-triggered mucocutaneous eruption with fever, ocular/oral involvement, targetoid macules, bullae, positive Nikolsky sign, and palm/sole involvement strongly indicates Stevens-Johnson syndrome—core knowledge for general dermatologists.

Classic travel-associated cutaneous larva migrans/strongyloidiasis presentation with serpiginous perianal lesions and eosinophilia, where identification of rhabditiform larvae in stool is standard core knowledge for general dermatologists.
Identifying vertical growth phase (Breslow depth) as the key prognostic factor for melanoma metastasis is core dermatology knowledge.
Requires recognizing disseminated varicella-zoster in an immunocompromised patient on ABVD and knowing the indication for inpatient IV acyclovir rather than outpatient antibiotics or scabicide.
This tests fundamental medical ethics (respect for patient autonomy and exploring preferences), which any practicing dermatologist should readily know regardless of subspecialty.

Classic pediatric HSP/IgA vasculitis after URI with palpable purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain; hematuria from IgA nephropathy is a well-known associated finding.

Identifying ACE-inhibitor–associated or hereditary angioedema with bradykinin mechanism and selecting danazol for long-term prophylaxis (vs acute therapies like FFP/ecallantide or unrelated metformin cessation) requires nuanced knowledge of angioedema subtypes and prophylactic options beyond basic dermatology fundamentals.

Recognizing that intrinsic/photoaging leads to decreased/elastin degeneration with reduced elastic fiber assembly causing laxity and fine periorbital wrinkles is core dermatology knowledge, while the distractors are less consistent with classic skin aging changes.

Recognizing Mohs micrographic surgery as the preferred next step for incompletely excised cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma on the nose (a high-risk, cosmetically sensitive site) is core dermatology management knowledge.
Recognizing lymphatic filariasis (elephantiasis) with nocturnal microfilaremia and knowing mosquitoes transmit Wuchereria bancrofti is standard core knowledge for general dermatologists.
Classic Kawasaki disease presentation in a toddler with mucocutaneous findings and prolonged fever, where the well-known feared complication is coronary artery aneurysms.
Classic tinea corporis presentation—annular, enlarging, pruritic plaque with animal exposure—readily recognized by general dermatologists.
Recognizing infantile hemangioma in a young child with congenital-onset, painless facial vascular lesions is classic core knowledge easily distinguished from warts, spider angiomas, and molluscum.

Identifying oculocutaneous albinism due to tyrosinase deficiency and knowing that hair bulb assays assess tyrosinase activity using DOPA substrate requires specific, less-common diagnostic knowledge beyond core clinical recognition.

Identifying bilateral hand burns from painless injury with suspended pain/temperature loss pointing to cervicothoracic syringomyelia requires cross-disciplinary neuro-derm reasoning beyond routine dermatology knowledge.
Recognizing that numerous atypical/dysplastic nevi increase melanoma risk and identifying melanoma histology as S100-positive epithelioid cells is core dermatology knowledge.
Identifying TEN from widespread desquamation after TMP-SMX exposure and distinguishing it from SJS by body surface area involvement is classic core knowledge for general dermatologists.
Identifying nonbullous impetigo in a child and selecting topical mupirocin as first-line therapy is core pediatric dermatology knowledge for general dermatologists.

Recognizing typical vitiligo features, its association with autoimmune disease, and that it often progresses slowly with occasional spontaneous repigmentation while knowing topical steroids are appropriate first-line for limited disease are core dermatology knowledge.
Recognizing that scarring after varicella lesions reflects the healing phase of acute inflammation is core pathology/dermatology knowledge that a general dermatologist would recall readily.
Recognition of mycosis fungoides from classic features—erythroderma with well-demarcated patches, pruritus, lymphadenopathy, and biopsy showing Pautrier microabscesses—is core dermatology knowledge.

Recognizing a delayed-type (Type IV) hypersensitivity reaction with indurated hypopigmented patch after intradermal antigen and linking it to Th1-mediated cellular immunity is core immunology knowledge routinely applied in dermatology (e.g., tuberculin testing).
Classic presentation of anogenital warts with aceto-whitening indicating condyloma acuminata due to HPV, a core dermatology diagnosis.
Recognizing trichotillomania with stress-related hair pulling and treating first-line with cognitive-behavioral therapy/behavior modification is core knowledge for general dermatologists.

Classic presentation of bullous pemphigoid (elderly, pruritus, tense bullae, negative Nikolsky sign, no mucosal involvement) with hallmark DIF finding of linear IgG and C3 at the basement membrane—core dermatology knowledge.
Recognizing xanthomas and xanthelasma and ordering a lipid panel to evaluate for hyperlipidemia is core dermatology knowledge.

Recognizing actinic keratosis as the classic precursor to cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma is core dermatology knowledge.

Identifying topical 5-fluorouracil as an FDA-approved therapy for superficial basal cell carcinoma and recalling its S-phase–specific inhibition of thymidylate synthase requires specific pharmacologic knowledge beyond basic dermatology fundamentals.

Identifying reactive arthritis with circinate balanitis and keratoderma blennorrhagicum and linking it to HLA-B27 as the key risk factor requires solid training beyond basic dermatology, though not subspecialty-level depth.

Ecthyma gangrenosum in a neutropenic chemotherapy patient is a classic presentation of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, where Exotoxin A is the key virulence factor causing tissue necrosis—core knowledge for general dermatologists.

Managing pediculosis capitis includes treating close contacts/household members with topical pediculicides like ivermectin to prevent reinfestation, a core, commonly known practice in general dermatology.

Recognizing Job (hyper-IgE) syndrome from eczema, recurrent staph abscesses, pneumonias, coarse facies, high IgE/eosinophilia, and TH17 deficiency—and linking it to defective neutrophil chemotaxis—requires immunology knowledge beyond routine dermatology, though still familiar to well-trained dermatologists.
Recognition of palmar erythema and spider angiomas in cirrhosis as estrogen-mediated vascular changes is classic core knowledge for general dermatology.

Identifying perianal condyloma acuminata (whitening with acetic acid) and choosing a standard destructive therapy like curettage is core dermatology knowledge, while the other options correspond to herpes, dermatitis, or syphilis, which are not consistent with the presentation.

Recognizing classic cat-scratch disease with localized tender lymphadenopathy after a kitten scratch and knowing that it is typically self-limited and does not require antibiotics is core dermatology knowledge.

Classic extensor plaques with silvery scale that bleed when scratched (Auspitz sign) point to psoriasis, whose hallmark is increased keratinocyte proliferation—core knowledge for general dermatologists.

Identifying neutrophils as the predominant cells 4–6 hours after an acute inflammatory insult is core pathology/dermatology knowledge applicable to common urticarial or arthropod-related reactions with systemic symptoms.
Classic basal cell carcinoma features (pearly/rolled border with central ulcer) on a small lesion are managed with excisional biopsy, a standard first-line step well known to general dermatologists.
Classic toxic shock syndrome from tampon use with fever, hypotension, diffuse rash is caused by staphylococcal superantigen leading to polyclonal T-cell activation.
Recognizing periorbital xanthelasma and knowing to screen with a fasting lipid profile alone is core dermatology knowledge without requiring additional tests.

The presentation is classic for vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) in an alcoholic with perifollicular petechiae and corkscrew hairs, and linking it to impaired hydroxylation of proline in collagen is core dermatology knowledge.

Recognizing that elastin’s elasticity derives from desmosine cross-links formed between lysine residues is core connective tissue biology commonly recalled by general dermatologists, with other options describing collagen features.
Classic presentation of Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) with perianal itching and positive tape test; mebendazole is a first-line, well-known treatment for general dermatologists.

Recognizing glucagonoma from the triad of weight loss, diabetes, diarrhea, and characteristic necrolytic migratory erythema with periorificial/genital lesions requires solid dermatology training and endocrine-derm pattern recognition beyond basic core knowledge.

Recognizing gummatous tertiary syphilis with granulomatous necrosis (gummas) and distinguishing it histologically from primary chancre (plasma cell–rich infiltrate) or secondary lesions requires nuanced staging knowledge beyond core basics.

Classic tinea cruris presentation with sparing of scrotum and sharply demarcated border; first-line topical allylamine like terbinafine is standard knowledge, while nystatin is ineffective for dermatophytes and steroid combos are discouraged.
Recognizing HPV-related genital warts with koilocytosis and the associated increased risk of cervical carcinoma is fundamental knowledge for any general dermatologist.

Identifying cherry angiomas—common, bright red papules on the trunk that may bleed when traumatized—is core dermatology knowledge with classic features distinguishing them from the listed alternatives.
Recognizing nonbullous impetigo with honey-colored crusts and its association with post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (elevated anti-DNase B) is core dermatology knowledge.
Classic presentation of Stewart-Treves syndrome (lymphangiosarcoma) arising in long-standing post-mastectomy lymphedema with violaceous plaques, a well-known association for general dermatologists.
Recognizing recurrent mucocutaneous candidiasis with onychomycosis as due to impaired cell-mediated immunity (T-cell dysfunction) is core immunology/dermatology knowledge for general dermatologists.

Classic presentation of bullous pemphigoid—tense, subepidermal blisters without mucosal involvement and negative Nikolsky sign—requiring recall that antibodies target hemidesmosomal proteins linking keratin intermediate filaments to the basement membrane (type IV collagen).
Classic presentation of hand-foot-and-mouth disease with oral ulcers and palm vesicles in a child, for which supportive care is standard; other options are clearly inappropriate.
Recognizing oral candidiasis from inhaled corticosteroid use and that plaques are scrapable is core, commonly tested knowledge for general dermatologists.
Recognizing that severe nodulocystic acne in a sexually active adolescent warrants isotretinoin and thus pregnancy testing beforehand is core dermatology knowledge.
Classic presentation and histology of superficial spreading melanoma (radial growth with atypical melanocytes at the DE junction and pagetoid spread) are core dermatology knowledge.
Recognizing classic newborn stigmata of Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) is fundamental pediatric dermatology knowledge for general dermatologists and does not require nuanced or rare details.
Classic presentation of bullous pemphigoid (tense blisters, negative Nikolsky sign, no mucosal involvement) with linear IgG/C3 at the basement membrane is core dermatology knowledge.
Identifying tinea versicolor by KOH showing hyphae and yeast (“spaghetti and meatballs”) and selecting topical selenium sulfide as first-line therapy is core dermatology knowledge.

Classic scarring alopecia with erythematous scaly plaques, dyspigmentation, pain/pruritus, and systemic lupus-like symptoms clearly points to DLE over non-scarring options like alopecia areata, tinea capitis, or trichotillomania.

Recognizing a pruritic back/flank rash in a young woman with chronic GI symptoms and elevated tTG as dermatitis herpetiformis due to gluten sensitivity is classic core knowledge for general dermatology.
Identifying a stage 1 pressure injury in an immobilized, hospitalized patient and choosing repositioning as first-line management is core dermatology knowledge.

Recognizing lymphocutaneous spread with nodular/bullous lesions after gardening as sporotrichosis and recalling itraconazole as first-line therapy requires specific, less-common infection knowledge beyond core derm topics.
Recognizing sunburn despite initial application and knowing that sunscreen must be reapplied after water exposure are core counseling points every dermatologist routinely knows.
Recognizing vitiligo and its mechanism of autoimmune destruction of melanocytes by autoreactive T cells is core dermatology knowledge with classic differentials easily excluded.

Recognizing photosensitive, nonpruritic blistering with hypertrichosis and dark urine as porphyria cutanea tarda and knowing low-dose hydroxychloroquine as first-line therapy (vs hemin for acute hepatic porphyrias, steroids/antihistamines not indicated) requires solid but somewhat specialized knowledge.

Classic lymphocutaneous spread after thorn injury (“rose gardener’s disease”) leading to sporotrichoid nodules is a well-known presentation any general dermatologist should readily recognize as sporotrichosis.
Recognizing that the decoy TNF-α receptor (etanercept) used for psoriasis/psoriatic arthritis increases risk of latent TB reactivation is core dermatology knowledge.

Classic presentation of staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome in a young child—fever, conjunctivitis, widespread desquamation sparing mucous membranes after impetigo—points directly to Staphylococcus aureus exotoxin, a well-known core diagnosis for general dermatologists.

Classic acute sunburn after UV exposure causing epidermal keratinocyte apoptosis (sunburn cells) is core dermatology knowledge easily distinguished from urticaria, immune complex disease, or delayed-type hypersensitivity.
Recognizing a nodular basal cell carcinoma on the eyelid and knowing Mohs micrographic surgery is first-line for cosmetically and functionally sensitive areas is core dermatology knowledge.
Identifying a painless, firm, rubbery nodule inside the eyelid as a chalazion is classic core knowledge for general dermatology and ophthalmologic-adjacent conditions.

Classic varicella-zoster/herpes virus presentation in an unvaccinated, immunosuppressed child with dermatomal painful vesicular rash, where Tzanck smear/biopsy shows multinucleated giant cells with intranuclear inclusions—core dermatology knowledge.
Classic presentation of leprosy with hypopigmented, anesthetic patch and raised borders in an immigrant from an endemic area, a core recognition expected of general dermatologists.

Identifying warfarin-induced skin necrosis and linking it to protein C deficiency (a natural anticoagulant) requires recognizing the clinical presentation, recent anticoagulant initiation, and the specific pathophysiology beyond basic dermatology knowledge.

Recognizing erythema multiforme major from clinical context and linking it to a biopsy showing an interface dermatitis with a rich lymphocytic (CD4+) infiltrate requires solid training beyond basic facts and includes distinguishing it from bullous disorders and other dermal infiltrate patterns.
Classic presentation of primary genital herpes with multiple painful shallow ulcers and tender lymphadenopathy, a core STI diagnosis for general dermatologists.

Classic presentation of genital warts (condyloma acuminata) where first-line, readily recalled treatments like cryotherapy or topical agents are appropriate; recognizing cryotherapy as a common initial management is core dermatology knowledge.
Classic infantile atopic dermatitis presentation with xerosis and pruritus on face/extensors and groin sparing; first-line management with topical emollients is core dermatology knowledge.
Classic tinea capitis in a child with alopecia, pruritic scaly patch, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy—requires systemic therapy with oral terbinafine, a core dermatology teaching.

Linking melanoma (from neural crest–derived melanocytes) to another neural crest tumor such as neuroblastoma requires embryologic knowledge beyond routine dermatology practice, though still within solid specialist training.

Classic localized, sharply demarcated erythema at the site of exposure (wrist) points to contact dermatitis over atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, or scabies—core pattern recognition for general dermatologists.
Recognizing a longstanding, stable, strawberry-colored raised nodule as a capillary hemangioma is classic core dermatology knowledge.
Classic seborrheic keratosis presentation with hallmark histology of immature keratinocytes and horn cysts is core dermatology knowledge.

Classic description of dermatitis herpetiformis with granular IgA at dermal papillae and extensor grouped vesicles, which is strongly associated with gluten (gliadin)-sensitive celiac disease—a core dermatology association.

Identifying bacillary angiomatosis in an AIDS patient from clinical clues and Warthin-Starry staining and recalling erythromycin as first-line therapy requires solid infectious derm knowledge beyond routine basics but is familiar to trained dermatologists.

Selecting 'Further questioning' requires recognizing that a small, brown lesion with a slightly raised border could represent a dermatofibroma or benign nevus and that history (e.g., duration, change, symptoms like dimpling) guides whether biopsy is needed, reflecting nuanced clinical judgment rather than rote management.
Recognizing multiple cherry angiomas and knowing they commonly increase in number with age is core dermatology knowledge, while the other options reflect misconceptions.
Classic presentation of xeroderma pigmentosum with UV sensitivity and early SCC requiring recall that nucleotide excision repair via excision endonuclease is defective.
Identifying a nonhealing, erythematous scaly ulcerated plaque as squamous cell carcinoma is core dermatology knowledge with classic features and straightforward differentials.
Classic presentation of xeroderma pigmentosum in an infant with severe photosensitivity and freckling points to defective nucleotide excision repair, a well-known core dermatology fact.
Recognizing congenital dermal melanocytosis (Mongolian spots) and providing reassurance without further workup is core dermatology knowledge.

Recognizing angiosarcoma arising in chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves syndrome) requires recalling a less-common but classic association and distinguishing it from other vascular or pigmented tumors.

Classic presentation and biopsy description (“swarm of bees” peribulbar lymphocytes) of alopecia areata that a general dermatologist would recognize readily, with straightforward exclusion of tinea capitis and other alopecias.
Recognizing SLE from malar rash, photosensitivity, systemic symptoms, anti-Smith antibodies, and linking pathogenesis to defective clearance of apoptotic debris is core dermatology knowledge.

Identifying Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans) in a young heavy smoker with distal ulcers and tobacco extract hypersensitivity, and knowing it involves segmental vasculitis of small and medium-sized arteries, is core dermatology knowledge.
Classic painless, indurated penile chancre indicating primary syphilis, confirmed by a treponemal test like FTA-ABS, is core dermatology knowledge.

Identifying porphyria cutanea tarda from photosensitive blisters with tea-colored urine and linking it specifically to uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase requires solid dermatology training and heme pathway enzyme recall beyond basic core knowledge.

Unilateral, chronic, nonpitting leg edema with thickened skin after travel to an endemic area points to filarial lymphedema from lymphatic obstruction, a classic presentation readily recognized by general dermatologists.
Associating pediatric obsessive-compulsive disorder with Tourette’s syndrome is a well-known core linkage in general practice and dermatology board contexts.
Recognizing oral thrush with odynophagia as a cue to evaluate for immunosuppression and order a CD4 count is core dermatology knowledge involving classic presentation and first-line workup.
Classic presentation of external genital warts (HPV) with acetic acid whitening and painless rough papules; first-line treatments like cryotherapy are core knowledge for general dermatologists.
Classic presentation of anogenital warts (condyloma acuminata) with aceto-whitening and painless papilliform lesions caused by low-risk HPV types 6 and 11 is core dermatology knowledge.
Identifying terbinafine’s primary mechanism (squalene epoxidase inhibition) for onychomycosis is core pharmacology commonly recalled by general dermatologists.

Classic presentation of tuberculoid leprosy with anesthetic hypopigmented patch and peripheral neuropathy in an immigrant, with standard first-line multidrug therapy (rifampin and dapsone) that a general dermatologist should readily recognize.
The vignette points to PCOS (irregular menses, acne, obesity, acanthosis nigricans, androgenic alopecia) and requires recalling that excess LH stimulates theca interna cells to produce androgens.
Recognizing that apocrine glands are responsible for puberty-related body odor is core dermatologic knowledge.
Recognizing café-au-lait macules with axillary/ophthalmic Lisch nodules and family history as NF1 and knowing neurofibromas are the associated neoplasms is core dermatology knowledge.

Classic presentation of tinea versicolor with hypopigmented, fine-scaling macules on the trunk that don’t tan, a common diagnosis and core knowledge for general dermatologists.
Classic unilateral eczematous/ulcerative nipple-areolar lesion with discharge and no systemic infection signs points to Paget disease, a well-known board staple for general dermatologists.

Recognizing Langerhans cell histiocytosis from oral ulcers, scaly rash, anemia, and lytic skull lesions and knowing CD1a (and often S100/Langerin) as the confirmatory marker requires solid dermatology training beyond basic core knowledge.

Classic presentation of leukocyte adhesion deficiency (delayed umbilical cord separation, recurrent bacterial infections, poor wound healing) tied to absent CD18 is core immunology knowledge commonly recognized by general dermatologists.
Classic scabies presentation with nocturnal pruritus and burrows in interdigital spaces; first-line treatment with permethrin is standard core knowledge.
Classic warfarin-induced skin necrosis shortly after initiation due to rapid decline in protein C levels is core dermatology knowledge.

Recognizing classic umbilicated papules of molluscum contagiosum and distinguishing them from cellulitis, HPV warts, or VZV is core dermatology knowledge.

Classic presentation of herpes zoster ophthalmicus with periocular vesicular rash requiring prompt systemic antiviral therapy is core knowledge for general dermatologists.

Classic pemphigus vulgaris presentation (painful oral erosions, flaccid bullae, positive Nikolsky sign) with pathogenesis of IgG against desmogleins (intercellular desmosomes) is core dermatology knowledge.
Identifying erythema migrans from Ixodes tick exposure and knowing Ixodes also transmits Babesia microti is core dermatology and general medicine knowledge.

Recognizing Kaposi sarcoma in an immunocompromised patient with violaceous mucocutaneous lesions and spindle-cell vascular proliferation due to HHV-8 is classic core dermatology knowledge.
Classic presentation of molluscum contagiosum in a child with umbilicated papules and standard first-line options like cryotherapy or topical podophyllotoxin are well-known to general dermatologists.
